text.p: Merging several European currencies may be easier than some people think, according to a man who helped steer Britain through a monetary transition of its own 26 years ago.

Noel Moore, who served on a British committee charged with smoothing the path for decimalisation in 1971, told Reuters there was no reason why the logistics of introducing the euro should prove unduly troublesome.
"The move to a single currency can be done, and done smoothly, if it is thought right to do it on political and economic grounds," he said in a recent interview.
"However, you really need to take decisions very soon and having made them, stick to them. You have to know exactly what you are going to have and when you are going to introduce it."

While Britain may be on the sidelines for the initial round of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), the British experience of a monetary transition is one of the few practical examples of how to tackle such a major project successfully.
The euro is due to be introduced on January 1, 1999, but the overall transition to the single currency from its member units takes place over a three-year period.

Setting aside the thorny problem of which countries will actually meet the criteria for monetary union, the practicalities of changing currencies will be magnified for EMU compared with British decimalisation.

Whereas for decimalisation, most bank notes and some of the higher value coins were kept in circulation, the move to the euro will involve not only a greater number of currencies but also the need to change all banknotes and coins within participating countries.

However this will be partially offset by the two-part transition. The European Central Bank is due to take over the operation of euro monetary policy in January 1999, but the issuance of euro banknotes and coins will not start until January 2002.
The euro is intended to run concurrently with domestic currencies until July 2002.

Moore, who was secretary of the British Decimal Currency Board during the transition to decimalisation and, prior to that secretary to Lord Halsbury's committee of enquiry on decimal currency, said in particular there needed to be widespread publicity given to conversion tables.
Publicity to raise awareness about the euro has so far been variable. Seen as largely the responsibility of national governments, it has depended in part on public enthusiasm for the project.

Some efforts have also been made by the European Commission. For instance, this year the commission has sent a boat up the river Rhine containing a floating exhibition to sell the advantages of the euro to a broadly sceptical German public.
Britain remains undecided on whether to participate in EMU but the chances of it joining in the first wave are considered extremely slim as the launch date is now less than a year and a half away.
Nevertheless, the new Labour government has initiated a wider debate on the pros and cons of EMU with the aim of making both the business community and the public better informed.
But some people believe with the notes and coins not due to be introduced until 2002, it is too soon to start raising public awareness.
Moore said decimalisation had benefited from a well publicised conversion table which he saw as the primary defence against any possibility of price increases.

"There is no doubt that people feared prices might go up as a result of decimalisation and were therefore unusually wary in assessing prices. But on the whole the operation went so smoothly that there were far fewer complaints afterwards than one would have expected," he said.
